title: TLS, SRTP, identity, and abuse
summary: Defensive digest, TLS certificates, SRTP keying, privacy headers, STIR, and abuse controls.

lessons.title: 401, 407, and digest
lessons.summary: A 401 from a UAS is answered with Authorization. A 407 from a proxy is answered with Proxy-Authorization.
objectives: Pair 401 with Authorization and WWW-Authenticate
Pair 407 with Proxy-Authorization and Proxy-Authenticate
Stop at the header split and do not compute an attack

illustration.title: Which challenge uses which header
illustration.caption: RFC 3261 section 22 is the SIP rule. RFC 7616 is the HTTP digest specification for algorithms.

paragraphs: RFC 3261 section 22 defines SIP digest and the two challenge statuses that use it. A UAS that needs to authenticate the user sends 401 Unauthorized and a WWW-Authenticate header, and the client retries with Authorization.

A proxy that needs to authenticate the user sends 407 Proxy Authentication Required and a Proxy-Authenticate header, and the client retries with Proxy-Authorization. A 401 does not ask for Proxy-Authorization, and a 407 does not ask for Authorization.

The challenge names the realm and the algorithm. RFC 7616 is the HTTP digest specification that adds algorithms such as SHA-256, and many challenges still show an older algorithm, so you read the parameter instead of assuming SHA-256.

The Authorization or Proxy-Authorization header carries a digest response, not the password in the clear. This lesson stops at which header answers which status. It does not compute that digest and it does not describe an attack.

fault.title: 401 retried with the proxy header
fault.symptom: A UAS returned 401 with WWW-Authenticate. The next INVITE adds only Proxy-Authorization, and the UAS challenges again.
fault.log:
SIP/2.0 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Digest realm="example.com", nonce="c0ffee02", algorithm=SHA-256, qop="auth"
next request has Proxy-Authorization and no Authorization
choices: A 401 is answered with Authorization, not with Proxy-Authorization
401 and 407 use the same client header
SHA-256 means the password is written in SDP
fault.why: RFC 3261 section 22 splits the UAS challenge from the proxy challenge.
fault.cause: The client treated every digest challenge as a proxy challenge.
fault.fix: On 401, send Authorization built for that WWW-Authenticate challenge. On 407, send Proxy-Authorization. Read the algorithm from the challenge. Do not place the password in the trace.

lessons.title: TLS and domain certificates
lessons.summary: SIP over TLS is RFC 3261 section 18. The certificate has to identify the SIP domain, per RFC 5922.
objectives: Treat TLS as a transport for the same SIP messages
Check the certificate against the SIP domain
Refuse a name that is only a nearby web host

illustration.title: What TLS is protecting
illustration.caption: TLS covers the SIP messages on that connection. It does not by itself choose SRTP.

layers.name: Certificate
layers.detail: Must identify the SIP domain, RFC 5922

paragraphs: RFC 3261 section 18 allows SIP over TLS. The request line and the headers are the same protocol, the Via transport token is TLS, and the usual port is 5061.
A sip URI with transport=tls and a sips URI both tell you to expect TLS, and they are not a statement that the media is SRTP. Media protection is negotiated in SDP and is a later lesson.

sections.h: The certificate names the SIP domain
paragraphs: RFC 5922 requires the certificate to identify the SIP domain the client intended to reach. Compare that identity with example.com when example.com is the domain you looked up, and reject a certificate that only names a different host.

A certificate for files.example.com does not identify the SIP domain example.com. Operators confirm the name with the peer's documented domain before they enable the trunk, and they do not accept a raw address that was never in the certificate.

lessons.title: SRTP and two keying methods
lessons.summary: SRTP is RFC 3711. SDES a=crypto is RFC 4568. DTLS-SRTP is RFC 5764. An SBC must not assume peers share one method.
objectives: Separate SRTP from the way keys are obtained
Name SDES and DTLS-SRTP as different keying methods
Key each SBC leg with the method that leg negotiated

illustration.title: Packet protection versus keying
illustration.caption: Copying one leg's keying line onto the other leg is the failure this lesson prevents.
rows: DTLS on the media path, fingerprint in SDP

sections.h: SRTP is not the key exchange
paragraphs: RFC 3711 defines SRTP, which encrypts and authenticates RTP and keeps the sequence number, timestamp, and SSRC in the packet. The profile token RTP/SAVP is SRTP, and it does not interchange with RTP/AVP.

Keying is a separate decision from the SRTP packet format itself. SDES, RFC 4568, puts the keying material in an a=crypto line inside SDP, so that line is only as private as the signaling path that carries it, and you use it on TLS when you use it at all.

DTLS-SRTP, RFC 5764, runs DTLS on the media path and derives the SRTP keys there. SDP carries a fingerprint so each side can check the certificate used in that handshake, and the profile token is UDP/TLS/RTP/SAVP rather than a bare RTP/AVP line.

An SBC must not assume two peers share one keying method. If one leg offers SDES and the other offers DTLS-SRTP, the SBC keys each leg with the method that leg negotiated and does not paste a=crypto onto the DTLS leg or paste a fingerprint onto a peer that asked for SDES.

quiz.why: 4568 and 5764 are keying methods. 3711 is the protected RTP.

quiz.why: The keying material rides in SDP, so the signaling path has to protect it.

quiz.q: DTLS-SRTP is
quiz.why: Keys come from DTLS on the media path. SDP carries a fingerprint.

quiz.why: RTP/SAVP is SRTP. RTP/AVP is not.

choices: Key each leg with the method that leg negotiated
Assume both peers already share one master key
quiz.why: The peers did not agree to one method. The SBC terminates and re-keys.

quiz.q: SDES keying material in SDP requires
choices: A protected signaling path, such as TLS, if you use SDES

DTLS-SRTP. Keys from DTLS. Fingerprint in SDP.

fault.symptom: Peer A negotiated SDES. Peer B negotiated DTLS-SRTP. The SBC forwarded Peer A's a=crypto line onto Peer B and media stays silent.

a=crypto and a fingerprint are the same method
Copying the line is required by RFC 3711
Silence means the SIP Call-ID collided
fault.why: SDES is RFC 4568. DTLS-SRTP is RFC 5764. SRTP itself is RFC 3711.
fault.cause: The SBC assumed the peers shared one keying method and pasted SDP keying from one leg onto the other.
fault.fix: Terminate media on the SBC and complete SDES only with the SDES peer and DTLS-SRTP only with the DTLS-SRTP peer. Keep key material out of tickets. Protect any SDES signaling with TLS.

lessons.title: Privacy and asserted identity
lessons.summary: Privacy is RFC 3323. P-Asserted-Identity and P-Preferred-Identity are for trusted networks, not cryptographic identity.
objectives: Name the Privacy header and the id token
Keep PAI and PPI inside a trust domain
Refuse to treat PAI as a signature

illustration.title: Trust domain boundary
illustration.caption: PPI is a hint from the UA. PAI is inserted by a trusted element. Both stop at the edge.

paragraphs: RFC 3323 defines the Privacy header and the tokens a user agent can set on it. The id token asks intermediaries to withhold a network-asserted identity, and other tokens cover headers, the session description, and user-level information.

Privacy: none means the user is not asking for those withholdings. If you do not understand a privacy token marked critical, you fail the request instead of forwarding an identity the user asked you to hide.

sections.h: Asserted identity is not a signature
paragraphs: RFC 3325 defines P-Asserted-Identity and P-Preferred-Identity for trusted networks. A user agent may send P-Preferred-Identity as a hint, and a trusted proxy that has authenticated the user may replace that hint with P-Asserted-Identity.

Outside the trust domain, remove both P-Asserted-Identity and P-Preferred-Identity before the request is forwarded. P-Asserted-Identity is not cryptographic identity, and it does not prove the caller to a carrier or to a user the way a signed token does, which is why STIR is the later lesson for that job.

lessons.title: STIR, PASSporT, and SHAKEN
lessons.summary: STIR is RFC 8224, PASSporT is RFC 8225, certificates are RFC 8226, and the SHAKEN extension is RFC 8588. Attestation levels are ATIS.
objectives: Point at the four RFCs for STIR, PASSporT, certificates, and SHAKEN
Require a verified Identity header before calling a call authenticated
Attribute attestation levels to ATIS and confirm the current document

illustration.title: What has to be present
illustration.caption: PAI is not a layer in this stack. Attestation levels are not invented here.

layers.name: RFC 8226
layers.detail: Certificates used to sign and verify

paragraphs: STIR, RFC 8224, puts a signed identity in the SIP Identity header. The token format is PASSporT, RFC 8225, and the certificates used with that signature are RFC 8226.

RFC 8588 is the SHAKEN PASSporT extension, and it is how a SHAKEN profile rides on the IETF token. Verification that fails, or an Identity header that is absent, means you do not present the From value as STIR-authenticated.

Attestation levels people label A, B, and C are an ATIS SHAKEN concept. They are defined by ATIS SHAKEN specifications, and you confirm the current ATIS document before you teach or display those levels. This lesson does not invent an ATIS document number or a date.

The FCC call-authentication page is the public regulator summary to cite beside those specifications. P-Asserted-Identity does not fill in for a missing Identity header, and a failed signature stays failed.

lessons.title: Scanning, hijack, and toll fraud
lessons.summary: Scanning, registration hijack, and toll fraud are classes of abuse. The response is authentication, exposure control, and alerting.
objectives: Recognize unsolicited SIP as scanning pressure on an open listener
Describe registration hijack as a replaced Contact binding
Treat toll fraud as unauthorized call completion

illustration.title: Class of abuse and the defensive control
illustration.caption: Each row is a failure mode a defender looks for. None of these rows is a procedure.
rows: INVITE and REGISTER from addresses you did not provision
Do not expose SIP to the whole Internet
Contact for an address-of-record changes unexpectedly
Authenticate REGISTER and alert on Contact changes
Calls complete from a source that is not allowed to place them
Authorize outbound calls. See the CME guide and FCC call authentication

paragraphs: An Internet-reachable SIP port receives unsolicited INVITE and REGISTER requests. That traffic is scanning for open services, and the defensive response is to accept SIP only from peers you named and to require authentication on REGISTER.

Registration hijack is the failure in which a Contact binding for an address-of-record is replaced, so later calls are routed to a target the user did not request. RFC 3261 requires the registrar to authenticate REGISTER. Alert when Contact changes to an address you did not provision.

Toll fraud is a class of abuse in which an unauthorized party completes calls that someone else pays for, and you treat it as an authorization failure. The Cisco CME toll-fraud prevention guide documents controls such as trusting only known sources.

Call authentication, summarized on the FCC call-authentication page, reduces spoofed caller identity and does not replace outbound authorization. This lesson names the classes and the controls, and it does not give steps for causing the abuse.

Log the source address, the method, the Request-URI, and whether a digest challenge was issued. A REGISTER that is stored with no challenge is a defect in the registrar configuration, and the fix is to refuse the binding.
Do not collect passwords into the ticket, and do not disable authentication to quiet an alarm. Pair this lesson with the hardening lesson for the allow list and the certificate check.

fault.fix: Reject sources you have not provisioned, require digest or TLS for peers you do accept, and keep outbound permissions separate from caller-ID authentication. Do not weaken authentication to clear the alarm.

lessons.title: Hardening a SIP edge
lessons.summary: A defensive edge limits peers, requires digest and TLS, strips PAI, and does not share SRTP keying across legs.
objectives: Write an allow list of signaling peers
Require digest on REGISTER and a domain certificate on TLS
Keep identity and media keying rules explicit

illustration.title: Controls that stack
illustration.caption: Each control answers a different failure. Removing one does not make the others optional.

sections.h: Who may speak SIP to you
paragraphs: Accept SIP from the peers you provisioned, such as 192.0.2.40 and 198.51.100.30 in this synthetic network, and refuse the rest. An open listener is the scanning condition from the threats lesson.

REGISTER is answered with 401 and WWW-Authenticate until Authorization checks out, and a proxy hop uses 407 and Proxy-Authorization. RFC 3261 section 22 and RFC 7616 are the references, and the password stays out of the configuration ticket.
Trunks that use TLS present a certificate that identifies the SIP domain, checked under RFC 5922, and a name mismatch stays a failed check. Do not override that failure to force the trunk up.

Strip P-Asserted-Identity at the trust boundary, and treat a call as STIR-authenticated only after the Identity header verifies. On media, key each leg with SDES or with DTLS-SRTP as that leg negotiated, and do not assume the peers share a method. The CME toll-fraud guide remains the product reference for trusted sources.

quiz.q: An edge allow list should
choices: Accept every source and sort it out in RTP
quiz.why: Unnamed sources are the scanning case.

quiz.why: A proxy challenge is the 407 case, with Proxy-Authorization.

quiz.why: It is not cryptographic identity.

quiz.why: Keep toll-fraud controls even when STIR is deployed.

cards.back: Named peers only. See the CME toll-fraud guide for trusted sources.

Certificate name equals the SIP domain.
Do not copy keying from one peer to another.

lab.title: Checklist, not a device stanza
lab.prompt: Read the teaching checklist. It is not a vendor configuration and it is not a router QoS policy.
steps: Name the RFC for the certificate line.
Name the header that answers a 407.

check.q: Which header answers a proxy challenge on this edge?
check.why: 407 uses Proxy-Authorization. 401 uses Authorization. Keep them split.

lab.config:
; Teaching checklist. Not a vendor stanza and not a router QoS policy.
; 1. Accept SIP only from 192.0.2.40 and 198.51.100.30.
; 2. Require digest on REGISTER. 401 uses Authorization. 407 uses Proxy-Authorization.
; 3. Require TLS. The certificate must identify example.com (RFC 5922).
; 4. Strip P-Asserted-Identity at the trust boundary.
; 5. Key each SRTP leg with the method that leg negotiated.
; 6. Do not mark a call STIR-authenticated without a verified Identity header.

fault.title: Authentication removed to stop an alarm
fault.symptom: Operators cleared a scanning alarm by accepting every REGISTER. A new Contact appears for alice@example.com.
fault.log:
policy change: digest disabled
REGISTER sip:example.com SIP/2.0
Contact: <sip:alice@192.0.2.40>
stored: yes
challenge: none
choices: Restoring digest and the peer allow list is the fix
Leaving digest off is required by RFC 5922
The Contact is a valid STIR attestation
fault.why: REGISTER without a challenge is how an unexpected Contact gets stored. That is the hijack class.
fault.cause: The edge traded a noisy alarm for unauthenticated bindings.
fault.fix: Turn digest back on, keep the allow list, and alert on Contact changes. Use the CME toll-fraud guide for trusted-source controls and keep FCC call authentication as a separate caller-identity control.
